title: Administrative recognition of autism in Chile
text:
0.1 What the report contains
This report describes how autism is recognised in the routine administrative records of Chile’s public health and education systems. It brings together every result the study produced, organised by what the result is about rather than by when it was computed.
Nothing here is prevalence or incidence. Every number is a count of hospital episodes, community programme entries, follow-up stocks or school enrolments, presented with its unit, its denominator and its coverage. The rise these records show is consistent with greater detection, greater demand and changes in coding during the period of Law 21.545; it does not demonstrate a change in how often autism occurs.
Methods. Sources, case definitions, units, denominators, standardisation, intervals, trends, spatial analysis, the rules for reading the monthly returns, quality controls, biases and limitations. It is the common reference for everything that follows.
Results. The principal findings: four panel figures and the nine supplementary figures that support them, each drawn at render time by the code printed with it.
Hospital recognition. The hospital discharge records in depth: magnitude and trend, age-standardised rates, sex and age, F84 subcategories, the diagnostic position of the code, episode characteristics, co-diagnoses, readmission, territory and spatial autocorrelation, and the reconstruction of which diagnoses precede the first observed autism record.
Community care. The monthly statistical returns of the public network: entries to and discharges from mental-health programmes with an autism code, their population rates, age, sex, regions, communes and facilities, screening in well-child check-ups, rehabilitation entries, and the ecological comparison between the two sources.
Result tables and extended plates hold the complete material, including the results that the main chapters summarise. Reproducibility explains how to rebuild every number in this report from the repository.

title: Administrative recognition of autism in Chile
text:
0.3 How this report was built
Every table and figure is recalculated when the report is rendered; none is pasted in. The chapters read the aggregated tables in output_files/consolidacion/ and docs/study/data/, both versioned in git, so the whole report can be rebuilt from a clone without the source microdata. The extraction from the original microdata runs separately, through the scripts documented in Reproducibility.
The study itself was written over several rounds of revision, which added results without ever changing one that had already been computed — a claim checked rather than asserted, by hashing every result table of every round and comparing them pairwise. This report presents the union of all of them as a single body of work. Where a result comes from a different observation window or an earlier case definition, the table says so on the spot.

title: 2  Methods
text:
2.1 Design and questions
This document describes, in one place, how every result of the community care and hospital recognition reports is built. Both chapters read aggregate tables produced by reproducible scripts and apply the same definitions, denominators and presentation conventions detailed here. When a result has a specific limitation, the corresponding report repeats it next to the table or figure; this section concentrates the full justification.
The work is a descriptive observational study based on administrative health records, with three complementary components:
The questions are framed in the classical person, place and time framework. No source identifies the incidence or prevalence of autism in the population: GRD records hospitalisations in which an F84 code was documented, and REM records aggregate counts of services. Measures are therefore always named by their real unit (records, identifiers, programme entries) and interpreted as indicators of contact with the public health system and of coding practice.

title: 2  Methods
text:
Descriptive epidemiology of hospital activity with an autism code (GRD, 2019–2024): magnitude, temporal trend, distribution by sex and age, diagnostic subcategories, position of the code in the episode, characteristics of the hospitalisation, co-diagnoses, readmission and territorial distribution, with population rates and spatial autocorrelation analysis.
Hospital coding trajectories (GRD, identifiers linked within 2019–2020 and 2021–2024): diagnoses recorded before the first observed autism record, principal or secondary position in the index episode and later transitions.
Outpatient care and screening activity (REM Series A, 2017–2024): entries to and discharges from mental-health programmes with an autism code, screening in well-child check-ups, rehabilitation and facility coverage, with population entry rates.

title: 2  Methods
text:
2.2 Epidemiological context
The most recent systematic reviews place the global prevalence of autism at around 1 in 100 people, with a median of 100 per 10,000 and a very wide range between studies, a median male:female ratio of 4.2 and one third of cases with concurrent intellectual disability (Zeidan et al. 2022). Meta-analyses with stricter criteria estimate lower pooled prevalences, of the order of 0.7% (Talantseva et al. 2023), while the Global Burden of Disease Study 2021 estimated 61.8 million autistic people, equivalent to 1 in 127, with an age-standardised prevalence of 788 per 100 000 (Santomauro et al. 2025). In the United States, ADDM surveillance reported 32.2 per 1,000 eight-year-old children in 2022, that is 1 in 31, with a prevalence more than three times higher in boys than in girls (Shaw et al. 2025).
The male:female ratio is considered overestimated by identification biases: the meta-analysis by Loomes and colleagues estimated a ratio close to 3:1 in studies that screen the general population, against 4.6:1 when only pre-existing diagnoses are counted (Loomes et al. 2017). Recent birth-cohort studies also show that the ratio decreases with age at diagnosis and with calendar period (Fyfe et al. 2026). Comorbidity is frequent and heterogeneous: attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder, anxiety, depression, epilepsy, intellectual disability, sleep disorders and gastrointestinal symptoms appear with very variable prevalences depending on the design (Bougeard et al. 2021). This background justifies presenting the sex ratio with intervals, stratifying by age and describing co-diagnoses without attributing a causal relation to them.
In Chile, population evidence is scarce. A study in two urban communes of Santiago applied M-CHAT screening to children aged 18 to 30 months with clinical confirmation by ADOS-2, estimating a prevalence of 1.95% (95% CI: 0.81 to 4.63) and four boys for every girl diagnosed (Yáñez et al. 2021). Law 21.545, published on 10 March 2023, established obligations of early detection, diagnosis and comprehensive care in health and education (Chile, Ministerio de Salud 2023). The study period therefore spans a regulatory change and a change in social visibility that must be considered when interpreting trends: an increase in records is compatible with greater detection, greater demand and coding changes, and does not by itself demonstrate an increase in the occurrence of autism.

title: 2  Methods
text:
2.3 Data sources

2.3.1 Hospital discharges grouped by GRD
The public database of diagnosis-related groups (IR-GRD, Grupos Relacionados por el Diagnóstico) of the Ministry of Health contains one record per episode of hospitalisation or major ambulatory surgery in the public facilities that take part in the GRD system (Ministerio de Salud de Chile 2025a). Each record includes sex, date of birth, commune of residence, health insurance, health service, hospital, admission and activity type, specialty, admission and discharge dates, discharge type, 35 diagnostic positions coded in ICD-10, 30 procedures, and the weight, severity and mortality risk assigned by the grouper. The canonical 2019–2024 files documented in the external data store are used; the files are neither modified nor copied into the repository.

The patient identifier is an encrypted field (CIP_ENCRIPTADO in 2019–2023, ID_BENEFICIARIO in 2024). The linkage audit verified that no identifiers are shared between 2019–2020 and 2021–2024, and that the change of field name in 2024 preserves matches with 2021–2023. All longitudinal analyses therefore work in two separate identifier periods and never link across 2020/2021. The stability of the identifier is an empirical check, not a certification by the producer.


2.3.2 Monthly Statistical Summaries (REM), Series A
REM (Resúmenes Estadísticos Mensuales) is the aggregate activity reporting system of the public network (Ministerio de Salud de Chile 2025b). Each row corresponds to a facility, month and service code, with up to 50 columns whose meaning depends on the form and the year. Three forms are used:

The annual dictionaries are read directly from the official files to assign the meaning of each column year by year; the catalogue rem_code_catalogue.csv keeps the file, sheet and dictionary row of each code. The 2025 and 2026 files exist but are not incorporated: 2026 is partial and 2025 requires validating integrity and comparability before extending the series.


2.3.3 Population denominators and cartography
The denominators are the INE population estimates and projections based on the 2017 Census, by commune, sex and single year of age, for 2017–2024 (Instituto Nacional de Estadísticas 2019). Ages are grouped into 17 five-year groups with an open group of 80 years and over. The population of a region or of the country is the sum of its communes. Multi-year pooled rates use person-years, that is, the sum of the annual populations of the period.
The commune cartography corresponds to the political-administrative division with 346 communes (unique territorial code, CUT) and the regional cartography to 16 regions, both in the EPSG:3857 projection. GRD records are assigned to the reported commune of residence; REM is assigned to the commune and region of the reporting facility. Non-continental communes (Easter Island, Juan Fernández, Antarctica and Cabo de Hornos) are kept in the tables but excluded from the contiguity statistics.

title: 2  Methods
text:
2.4 Case definitions

2.4.1 ICD-10 codes in GRD
Three nested definitions are used, identical in the descriptive epidemiology and in the trajectories:








Definition
ICD-10 codes
Use




Specific autism
F84.0
Restrictive sensitivity


Operational ASD
F84.0, F84.1, F84.5, F84.8, F84.9
Main definition in all results


Historical F84
F84 and all its valid subcategories, including F84.2, F84.3 and F84.4
Comparison with the full category of pervasive developmental disorders



The operational definition approximates the DSM-5 concept of autism spectrum disorder with the ICD-10 nomenclature (World Health Organization 2019), which still distinguishes childhood autism, atypical autism and Asperger syndrome; it is not an exact clinical equivalence. F84.2 (Rett syndrome), F84.3 (disintegrative disorder) and F84.4 (overactive disorder with mental retardation and stereotyped movements) are described separately as subcategories.
Codes are normalised by removing dots and spaces. A record is a case when any of the 35 diagnostic fields contains a code of the definition. The position is classified exclusively: principal when only DIAGNOSTICO1 contains the code, secondary only when it appears only in DIAGNOSTICO2 to DIAGNOSTICO35, and principal and secondary when it appears in both. This semantics is operational and should be confirmed with the producer’s dictionary; the reports use it consistently.


2.4.2 REM codes
The A05 codes of entry to the mental-health programme with an autism code (05990022) constitute the main series; Asperger (05990023), Rett (05990024), disintegrative disorder (05990025) and unspecified PDD (05990026) are presented as subcategories, and their corresponding discharges (05990027 to 05990031) separately. The generic series of pervasive developmental disorders of 2017–2020 (06902600 entries and 05225000 discharges) is kept without mixing it with the later subcategories. The A03 and A28 codes are listed in the REM report with their dictionary label.

title: 2  Methods
text:
2.6 Rates, standardisation and intervals

2.6.1 Crude and specific rates
For a set of \(d\) events and \(n\) person-years, the crude rate is \(r = 10^5 \cdot d / n\). The 95% confidence limits come from the exact Poisson interval for \(d\) through the chi-squared distribution, \(d_L = \chi^2_{2d,\,0.025}/2\) and \(d_U = \chi^2_{2d+2,\,0.975}/2\), divided by \(n\) (Breslow and Day 1987). Age- and sex-specific rates use the same rule.


2.6.2 Direct standardisation
Age-standardised rates (ASR) are calculated by the direct method with the WHO world standard population (Ahmad et al. 2001), collapsed to the group aged 80 and over:
\[\mathrm{ASR} = \sum_{i} w_i \, \frac{d_i}{n_i}, \qquad w_i = \frac{p_i}{\sum_j p_j}\]
where \(d_i\), \(n_i\) and \(p_i\) are the events, person-years and standard weight of age group \(i\). Groups without population are excluded and the weights are renormalised; groups without events contribute zero. The 95% intervals use the gamma method of Fay and Feuer (Fay and Feuer 1997), which respects the asymmetry of rates with few events:
\[\mathrm{Var}(\mathrm{ASR}) = \sum_i w_i^2 \frac{d_i}{n_i^2}, \qquad w_M = \max_i \frac{w_i}{n_i}\]
\[L = G^{-1}\!\left(0.025;\ \tfrac{\mathrm{ASR}^2}{\mathrm{Var}},\ \tfrac{\mathrm{Var}}{\mathrm{ASR}}\right), \qquad U = G^{-1}\!\left(0.975;\ \tfrac{(\mathrm{ASR}+w_M)^2}{\mathrm{Var}+w_M^2},\ \tfrac{\mathrm{Var}+w_M^2}{\mathrm{ASR}+w_M}\right)\]
with \(G^{-1}(q; a, b)\) the quantile of a gamma distribution with shape \(a\) and scale \(b\).

2.6.3 Rate ratio between sexes
The ratio between the male and female ASRs is accompanied by a log-normal interval, \(\exp\{\ln(\mathrm{RR}) \pm 1.96 \cdot \mathrm{se}\}\) with \(\mathrm{se}^2 = \mathrm{Var}_M/\mathrm{ASR}_M^2 + \mathrm{Var}_F/\mathrm{ASR}_F^2\). The male:female count ratio is presented with the exact conditional binomial interval (Clopper–Pearson on the proportion of males among cases). Both ratios describe the composition of the records and not the prevalence ratio of autism.


2.6.4 Indirect standardisation and empirical Bayes smoothing
For the commune analysis, where counts are small, the standardised hospitalisation ratio (SHR) is also calculated: the quotient between observed records and those expected if each commune had the national sex- and age-specific rates of the same period, with exact Poisson intervals (Ulm 1990). The ratios are smoothed with Marshall’s global empirical Bayes estimator (Marshall 1991): each SHR is shrunk towards the national ratio with a weight \(E_i/(E_i + m/v)\), where \(E_i\) are the expected events of the commune, and \(m\) and \(v\) the prior mean and variance estimated by the method of moments. The tables report the crude ratio, the smoothed ratio and the shrinkage weight; the maps and spatial statistics use the smoothed ratio to reduce the instability of small communes.


2.6.5 Trends
The temporal trend is summarised with the average annual percent change (AAPC) estimated with a log-linear count model with an offset of the logarithm of the population, \(\log E[d_t] = \alpha + \beta t + \log n_t\), so that \(\mathrm{AAPC} = 100\,(e^{\beta} - 1)\) (Clegg et al. 2009). Overdispersion is corrected with a Pearson scale factor (quasi-Poisson), which widens the intervals when the series departs from an exponential trend, as happens with the 2020 drop. Two periods are estimated: the full 2019–2024 period and 2021–2024, which coincides with the main identifier period and with the specific REM codes. Seasonality is described with monthly indices, the quotient between the mean of each month and the overall monthly mean.

title: 2  Methods
text:
2.7 Territorial and spatial analysis
Regional rates are calculated by region of residence (GRD) or of the facility (REM), annual and pooled, with direct standardisation and gamma intervals. Commune rates are pooled over the whole available period to gain stability: records 2019–2024 against person-years, and hospitalised persons 2021–2024 against the mean annual population of the period.
Global spatial autocorrelation is assessed with Moran’s I (Moran 1950) over the continental communes, with a row-standardised queen contiguity matrix and inference by 999 random permutations, with a fixed seed for reproducibility. Anselin’s local indicators of spatial association (LISA) (Anselin 1995) classify each commune into high-high, low-low, high-low and low-high quadrants; local significance is reported with the pseudo p-value of 999 permutations and, in addition, with a threshold corrected by the false discovery rate (Benjamini and Hochberg 1995), which is the recommended reading given the number of communes. The calculations use the PySAL library (Rey and Anselin 2010). Communes without neighbours (contiguous islands) remain on the map without contributing to the lags.
The spatial analysis is exploratory and ecological (Elliott et al. 2000): clusters of high rates may reflect hospital supply, coding practices, access and socioeconomic composition, and not a territorial risk of autism. The commune unit introduces the modifiable areal unit problem, and the commune of residence does not always coincide with the place of care.

title: 2  Methods
text:
2.8 Hospitalisation characteristics and co-diagnoses
Episode variables are described as distributions of records by year and code position: admission type, activity type, medical specialty, referral source, health insurance (grouped into FONASA MAI brackets, free choice, ISAPRE, Armed Forces, private and others), discharge type, severity and mortality risk of the grouper, GRD relative weight, hospital and health service. Length of stay is summarised with median, quartiles and the 90th percentile and stratified by activity type and age group, because major ambulatory surgery has a zero stay by definition.
Co-diagnoses are the codes other than F84 present in any position of the same record, summarised into three-character ICD-10 categories, chapters and mental-health blocks. When the autism code is secondary, the principal diagnosis describes the coded reason for the hospitalisation. These co-occurrences describe joint coding in an episode: they establish neither sequence, causality nor prevalence of comorbidity in the autistic population.

title: 2  Methods
text:
2.9 Hospital coding trajectories
The longitudinal component reconstructs, within each identifier period, all discharges of the identifiers with any F84 code. The index date is the first observed discharge with the selected definition; age is that at admission to that episode. A strict prior episode must have been discharged before admission to the index episode; overlapping or same-day episodes are quantified separately. The report describes the first observed principal diagnosis, the last prior principal diagnosis, prior codes and groups in 365-day, 730-day and whole-period windows, sequences without ties and the later step from secondary to principal, with proportions calculated only among those with 365 calendar days before the end of the period. Exclusions (identifiers with inconsistent birth date or sex, ambiguous episodes, invalid dates, implausible ages) are documented and not imputed. Observation opportunity is distinguished from clinical follow-up: having calendar time does not certify continuous observation, and the absence of prior hospitalisations does not imply the absence of outpatient diagnoses.

title: 2  Methods
text:
2.10 REM reading rules

A05. Col01 is the total, Col02 males and Col03 females; the 17 age groups occupy Col04 to Col37 in male/female pairs. Rates are calculated with the age and sex cells; the total Col01 may differ slightly when cells are missing.
A03. In the screening sections Col01 is males and Col02 females; from 2023 Col03 and Col04 correspond to Indigenous peoples and migrants and are not added to the total. The total of a row requires both sex columns; incomplete rows are counted separately.
A28. Col01 gathers both sexes; sections A.2 and B.1 are kept separate and are not added as distinct persons.
Facility panel. A facility reports a code in a month when a row exists; the absence of a row, the empty cell and the explicit zero are distinguished. A stable panel is defined as the set of facilities with at least one reported entry in each of the years 2021–2024, and serves to check that the trend does not depend solely on the incorporation of new reporters.
Screening indicators. Quotients are calculated only between codes of the same section, instrument, stage and age group. In the 2019–2022 series, abnormal screening among screenings performed is reported; in 2023–2024, the risk distribution of the first part of the M-CHAT R/F and the referral in the second part. None of these quotients is a population positivity, because the denominator is not all screened children.
Ecological comparison. Regional rates of REM entries and GRD hospitalisations are compared by region and year with Spearman correlation, as a description of the territorial coherence between sources with different units. At commune scale, where REM only provides totals by commune of the facility and GRD the commune of residence, crude rates per 100 000 person-years and indirect standardised ratios (observed over expected according to the national sex- and age-specific rates of the same source and period) are compared by year and for 2021–2024 pooled. The main analysis uses the continental communes with at least one facility reporting the code; as a sensitivity it is repeated among communes with at least 20 entries and 20 hospitalised persons and among all continental communes with zero imputed to non-reporting communes, since the absence of a REM row is not automatically interpreted as zero.

title: 2  Methods
text:
2.11 Data quality and controls
Each script writes control tables that the reports show next to the results: records read, exact duplicates removed, missing or invalid identifiers, invalid dates, implausible ages (negative or over 110 years), records without sex or age, communes not assigned to the INE catalogue, and in REM the consistency between the total and the sums by sex and age of complete rows. Communes of residence are linked to the unique territorial code by normalised name, with three documented aliases (Coyhaique, Concón and Aysén); only records with an “unknown” commune remain without a region. The analytical code has unit tests with synthetic data for the rules on dates, positions, prior episodes and ties, and for the rate and interval functions.

title: 2  Methods
text:
2.12 Biases and limitations

Selection. GRD covers hospitalisations in public facilities that take part in the GRD system; autistic people without a hospitalisation, cared for in the private system or in hospitals without GRD do not appear. The rates describe hospital activity with the code, not the occurrence of autism.
Detection and coding. The probability that an F84 code is recorded in a hospitalisation depends on clinical awareness, the availability of a prior diagnosis and coding rules. Law 21.545 and the increase in demand for assessment probably raised recording between 2021 and 2024 independently of changes in occurrence.
Left censoring. The first observed hospital record is not the first diagnosis; a person may have been diagnosed years earlier in outpatient care.
Denominators. The INE projections are estimates and do not incorporate the results of the 2024 Census; the commune of residence may be outdated or misreported.
REM comparability. Changes of codes (2021), screening instruments (2023) and sections (2024) prevent homogeneous series; the number of reporting facilities changes every year.
Ecological fallacy and areal unit. Territorial associations do not apply to persons and depend on the commune division.
Multiple comparisons. With more than 300 communes, reading with p < 0.05 produces false positives; the false discovery rate correction is preferred.
No causal inference. No risk or survival models are estimated; differences between groups are described without multivariable adjustment.

title: 2  Methods
text:
2.13 Ethics and data protection
The GRD and REM databases are public or of authorised use and contain no names. Encrypted identifiers are processed in memory and never exported; all tables in the repository are aggregates without identifiers, without individual dates and without combinations that would allow re-identification. Commune tables with small counts are published with their intervals to avoid over-interpretation.

title: 3  Results
text:
3.1 Panel figures
These are the principal results of the study: four panel figures that carry the main findings, nine supplementary figures that support them, and the tables they are built from. Every one is drawn here, at render time, by the code printed with it — nothing on this page is a stored image.
Case definition: hospital episodes with an eligible F84 code, excluding Rett syndrome (F84.2); community programmes with the strict autism code except where the “F84 family” is indicated. Every count is administrative recognition, not prevalence or incidence: a count of episodes, programme entries, follow-up stocks or school enrolments, each with its unit, its denominator and its coverage.
Use Show the code that produced this under any figure or table, or the </> Code button at the top right, to read the code that drew it. Each figure chunk exports the 175 mm PNG, SVG and PDF files to docs/study/figures/ as it runs, in English and Spanish, and displays the English plate.

def fig1(lang):
    style(); fig = plt.figure(figsize=(175/25.4, 215/25.4))
    top = fig.add_gridspec(1, 2, left=0.115, right=0.985, top=0.97, bottom=0.735, wspace=0.42)
    mid = fig.add_gridspec(1, 2, left=0.30, right=0.985, top=0.645, bottom=0.40, wspace=0.40, width_ratios=[1, 1.12])
    bot = fig.add_gridspec(1, 2, left=0.115, right=0.985, top=0.315, bottom=0.085, wspace=0.42)
    g = load_grd_summary()
    obs = g.query("panel=='observed' and position=='any'").set_index('year').reindex(YRS_GRD)
    fix = g.query("panel=='fixed65' and position=='any'").set_index('year').reindex(YRS_GRD)
    pri = g.query("panel=='observed' and position=='principal'").set_index('year').reindex(YRS_GRD)
    # (a) primary indicator per 100 000 GRD episodes
    a = fig.add_subplot(top[0, 0]); clean(a); shade_pandemic(a)
    for z, col, mk, ls, lab in [(obs, BLUE, 'o', '-', text('Any position, observed panel', 'Cualquier posición, observados', lang)),
                                (fix, BLACK, 's', '--', text('Any position, stable 65 hospitals', 'Cualquier posición, 65 estables', lang)),
                                (pri, ORANGE, 'D', '-', text('Principal diagnosis', 'Diagnóstico principal', lang))]:
        a.fill_between(z.index, z.rate_lo, z.rate_hi, color=col, alpha=0.15, lw=0)
        a.plot(z.index, z.rate_per_100k_episodes, color=col, marker=mk, ls=ls, label=lab, mfc='white' if mk == 's' else col, ms=3.2)
    log_axis(a, 'y', lang); a.set_ylim(10, 2500); year_ticks(a, YRS_GRD, short=True)
    a.set_ylabel(text('Eligible episodes per 100 000\nGRD episodes (log scale)', 'Episodios elegibles por 100 000\nepisodios GRD (escala log)', lang))
    a.legend(loc='upper left', handlelength=1.6, borderaxespad=0.2)
    end_label(a, 2024, obs.rate_per_100k_episodes[2024], num(obs.rate_per_100k_episodes[2024], lang, 1), BLUE, dy=-8)
    end_label(a, 2024, pri.rate_per_100k_episodes[2024], num(pri.rate_per_100k_episodes[2024], lang, 1), ORANGE, dy=-6)
    a.set_xlim(2018.6, 2024.9)
    # (b) age-standardised indicators per 100 000 residents by source
    b = fig.add_subplot(top[0, 1]); clean(b); shade_pandemic(b)
    pr = pd.read_csv(TIDY/'models_population_rates.csv').query("variant=='sin_rett' and position=='any' and sex=='TOTAL'").set_index('year').reindex(YRS_GRD)
    a05 = pd.read_csv(DATA/'models_a05_standardised_rates.csv').query("variant=='strict_autism' and sex=='TOTAL'").set_index('year').reindex(YRS_REM)
    b.fill_between(pr.index, pr.asr_lo, pr.asr_hi, color=BLUE, alpha=0.15, lw=0)
    b.plot(pr.index, pr.asr, color=BLUE, marker='o', label=text('GRD eligible episodes, any position', 'Episodios GRD elegibles, cualquier posición', lang))
    b.fill_between(a05.index, a05.asr_lo, a05.asr_hi, color=GREEN, alpha=0.15, lw=0)
    b.plot(a05.index, a05.asr, color=GREEN, marker='^', label=text('A05 strict-autism programme entries', 'Ingresos A05 por autismo estricto', lang))
    law_line(b, lang, y=0.22)
    b.set_ylim(0, 120); b.set_xlim(2018.6, 2025.6); year_ticks(b, range(2019, 2026), short=True)
    b.set_ylabel(text('Records per 100 000 residents,\nWHO age-standardised', 'Registros por 100 000 residentes,\nestandarizados por edad (OMS)', lang))
    b.legend(loc='upper left', handlelength=1.6, borderaxespad=0.2)
    end_label(b, 2024, pr.asr[2024], num(pr.asr[2024], lang, 1), BLUE, dy=-7)
    end_label(b, 2025, a05.asr[2025], num(a05.asr[2025], lang, 1), GREEN, dy=6, ha='right', dx=-2)
    # (c) annual percent change forest (half width, short labels)
    c = fig.add_subplot(mid[0, 0]); clean(c, grid='x')
    rows = load_forest(); groups = {'grd': text('Per 100 000 GRD episodes', 'Por 100 000 episodios GRD', lang),
                                    'pop': text('Per 100 000 residents, age-adjusted', 'Por 100 000 residentes, ajustado por edad', lang),
                                    'rem': text('REM programmes, 2021–25', 'Programas REM, 2021–25', lang)}
    y = 0.0; ticks = []; labels = []; last = None
    for grp, en, es, (apc, lo, hi, df), col, mk in rows:
        if grp != last:
            y += 0.6; c.text(-0.98, y, groups[grp], transform=c.get_yaxis_transform(), fontsize=6.9, fontweight='bold', va='center', ha='left', color='#333333', clip_on=False); y += 1.0; last = grp
        c.errorbar(apc, y, xerr=[[apc - lo], [hi - apc]], fmt=mk, color=col, ms=3.6, capsize=1.6, lw=0.85, mfc=col if mk in 'oD^v' else 'white')
        ticks.append(y); labels.append(text(*SHORT[en], lang)); y += 1.0
    c.set_yticks(ticks); c.set_yticklabels(labels, fontsize=6.8); c.set_ylim(y - 0.4, -0.2); c.invert_yaxis() if False else None
    c.axvline(0, color='#555555', lw=0.7, ls=':'); c.set_xlim(-5, 70); c.set_xticks([0, 20, 40, 60])
    c.set_xlabel(text('Annual percent change (95% CI)', 'Cambio porcentual anual (IC 95%)', lang))
    c.tick_params(axis='y', length=0)
    # (d) F80–F89 block comparator, per 100 000 GRD episodes
    d = fig.add_subplot(mid[0, 1]); clean(d); shade_pandemic(d)
    f8 = pd.read_csv(DATA/'f80_f89_episode_rates.csv')
    panel = 'observed' if (f8.panel == 'observed').any() else 'fixed65'; f8 = f8[f8.panel == panel]
    # The block tabulation counts the whole F84 family (with F84.2); the eligible F84 line is drawn
    # from the sin_rett series of grd_year_summary on the same observed panel and denominator.
    tot = f8.query("category=='F84' and year==2024").n_episodes_total.iloc[0]
    assert panel == 'observed' and int(tot) == int(obs.n_episodes_total_same_panel_activity[2024]), (panel, tot)
    order = ['F84', 'F80', 'F83', 'F82', 'F81', 'F89', 'F88']
    cols = {'F84': BLUE, 'F80': GREEN, 'F83': SKY, 'F82': GOLD, 'F81': PINK, 'F89': GREY, 'F88': '#8c6d31'}
    mks = {'F84': 'o', 'F80': 's', 'F83': 'D', 'F82': 'v', 'F81': '^', 'F89': 'x', 'F88': 'P'}
    for cat in order:
        z = f8[f8.category == cat].set_index('year').reindex(YRS_GRD)
        if cat == 'F84': z = obs
        d.plot(z.index, z.rate_per_100k_episodes, color=cols[cat], marker=mks[cat], ls='-' if cat == 'F84' else '--', lw=1.4 if cat == 'F84' else 1.0, ms=3.2, label=text(*F8X_LABELS[cat], lang))
    log_axis(d, 'y', lang); d.set_ylim(1, 2000); d.set_xlim(2018.6, 2024.6); year_ticks(d, YRS_GRD, short=True)
    d.set_ylabel(text('Episodes per 100 000 GRD\nepisodes (log scale)', 'Episodios por 100 000\nepisodios GRD (escala log)', lang)); d.set_ylim(1, 5000)
    d.legend(loc='upper left', ncol=2, handlelength=1.4, columnspacing=0.7, handletextpad=0.4, borderaxespad=0.15, fontsize=6.4)
    # (e) male:female ratio
    e = fig.add_subplot(bot[0, 0]); clean(e)
    sr = pd.read_csv(DATA/'fig3d_sex_ratios.csv')
    for src, col, mk, lab in [('GRD', BLUE, 'o', text('GRD eligible episodes', 'Episodios GRD elegibles', lang)), ('A05', GREEN, '^', text('A05 strict-autism entries', 'Ingresos A05 autismo estricto', lang))]:
        z = sr[sr.source == src].sort_values('year')
        e.fill_between(z.year, z.ratio_lo, z.ratio_hi, color=col, alpha=0.15, lw=0)
        e.plot(z.year, z.male_female_count_ratio, color=col, marker=mk, label=lab)
        end_label(e, z.year.iloc[-1], z.male_female_count_ratio.iloc[-1], num(z.male_female_count_ratio.iloc[-1], lang, 2), col, dy=(-8 if src == 'GRD' else -7))
        end_label(e, z.year.iloc[0], z.male_female_count_ratio.iloc[0], num(z.male_female_count_ratio.iloc[0], lang, 2), col, dx=(4 if src == 'GRD' else 0), dy=(8 if src == 'GRD' else 9), ha=('left' if src == 'GRD' else 'center'))
    shade_pandemic(e); law_line(e, lang, y=0.20)
    e.set_ylim(1, 4.3); e.set_xlim(2018.6, 2025.5); year_ticks(e, range(2019, 2026), short=True)
    e.set_ylabel(text('Male:female ratio of records\n(95% CI)', 'Razón hombre:mujer de los\nregistros (IC 95%)', lang))
    e.legend(loc='lower left', handlelength=1.6, borderaxespad=0.2)
    # (f) age-specific GRD rates, 2019 vs 2024, both sexes
    f = fig.add_subplot(bot[0, 1]); clean(f, grid='x')
    ar = load_age_rates('grd', 2019, 2024); groups_age = list(ar[2019].index); ypos = np.arange(len(groups_age))
    for i, gname in enumerate(groups_age):
        r0, r1 = ar[2019].loc[gname], ar[2024].loc[gname]
        f.plot([r0.rate, r1.rate], [i, i], color=LIGHT, lw=1.2, zorder=1)
        pct = (r1.rate / r0.rate - 1) * 100
        f.text(max(r0.rate, r1.rate) * 1.4, i, ('+' if pct >= 0 else '−') + num(abs(pct), lang, 0) + ' %', va='center', fontsize=6.6, color=ORANGE if pct >= 0 else BLUE)
    f.scatter(ar[2019].rate, ypos, s=18, facecolors='white', edgecolors=BLUE, linewidths=1.1, zorder=3, label='2019')
    f.scatter(ar[2024].rate, ypos, s=18, color=ORANGE, marker='s', zorder=3, label='2024')
    log_axis(f, 'x', lang); f.set_xlim(0.3, 4000); f.set_yticks(ypos); f.set_yticklabels([s.replace('-', '–') for s in groups_age]); f.invert_yaxis()
    f.set_xlabel(text('Eligible episodes per\n100 000 residents (log scale)', 'Episodios elegibles por\n100 000 residentes (escala log)', lang))
    f.set_ylabel(text('Age group (years)', 'Grupo de edad (años)', lang))
    f.legend(loc='lower right', handlelength=1.2, borderaxespad=0.2)
    for ax, ch in zip([a, b, c, d, e, f], 'abcdef'): letter(fig, ax, ch, dx=(-0.27 if ch == 'c' else -0.075))
    save(fig, 'Figure_1', lang, close=False)
    return fig

    sub_lab = {'total': text('Total', 'Total', lang), 'Hombre': text('Males', 'Hombres', lang), 'Mujer': text('Females', 'Mujeres', lang)}
    y = 0; ticks = []; labels = []
    for dom, en, es, col in blocks:
        c.text(0.04, y, text(en, es, lang), fontsize=6.6, fontweight='bold', color=col, va='center', ha='left', transform=c.get_yaxis_transform()); y += 1
        for sub in ['total', 'Hombre', 'Mujer']:
            r = sv[(sv.domain == dom) & (sv.subgroup == sub)].iloc[0]
            est, lo, hi = r.proportion * 100, r.lo * 100, r.hi * 100
            imp = str(r.precision_flag) != 'adequate'
            c.errorbar(est, y, xerr=[[est - lo], [hi - est]], fmt='o', color=LIGHT if imp else col, ms=3.4, capsize=1.6, lw=0.9)
            c.text(hi * 1.15, y, f'{num(est, lang, 2)} ({num(lo, lang, 2)}–{num(hi, lang, 2)})', va='center', fontsize=6.2, color='#555555' if imp else '#222222')
            ticks.append(y); labels.append(f'{sub_lab[sub]} · {int(r.cases)}/{num(int(r.n), lang)}'); y += 1
        y += 0.4
    c.set_yticks(ticks); c.set_yticklabels(labels, fontsize=6.4); c.set_ylim(y - 0.4, -0.7); c.tick_params(axis='y', length=0)
    log_axis(c, 'x', lang); c.set_xlim(0.07, 40); c.set_xticks([0.1, 0.3, 1, 3, 10]); c.xaxis.set_major_formatter(FuncFormatter(lambda v, p: num(v, lang, 1) if v < 1 else num(v, lang, 0)))
    c.set_xlabel(text('Weighted % with 95% CI (log scale); labels: cases/unweighted n\ngrey: imprecise (RSE > 30% or < 30 cases)', '% ponderado con IC 95% (escala log); etiquetas: casos/n sin ponderar\ngris: impreciso (RSE > 30% o < 30 casos)', lang), fontsize=6.8)
    # (d) commune-level comparison between hospital and programme indicators, 2021–2024
    d = fig.add_subplot(gs[1, 1]); clean(d, grid='both')
    # Public extract: rates of communes whose GRD and A05 counts are 0 or >= 5 (cells 1-4 masked); no identifiers.
    base = pd.read_csv(DATA/'communes_public.csv'); corr = pd.read_csv(DATA/'S4_correlations_selected_sensitivities.csv')
    z = base.dropna(subset=['GRD', 'A05'])
    rm = z.metropolitan.astype(bool)
    d.scatter(z.GRD[~rm], z.A05[~rm], s=12, color=BLUE, alpha=0.7, edgecolors='white', linewidths=0.3, label=text('Other regions', 'Otras regiones', lang), clip_on=False)
    d.scatter(z.GRD[rm], z.A05[rm], s=14, facecolors='white', edgecolors=ORANGE, linewidths=0.9, label=text('Metropolitan Region', 'Región Metropolitana', lang), clip_on=False)
    r = corr[(corr.pair == 'GRD–A05') & (corr.scope == 'commune') & (corr.analysis == 'core')].iloc[0]
    rx = corr[(corr.pair == 'GRD–A05') & (corr.scope == 'commune') & (corr.analysis == 'exclude_metropolitan')].iloc[0]
    d.text(0.02, 0.97, text(f'Spearman ρ = {num(r.rho, lang, 2)}; n = {int(r.n)}\nexcluding Metropolitan Region: ρ = {num(rx.rho, lang, 2)}; n = {int(rx.n)}\n{len(z)} communes shown; counts 1–4 suppressed',
                            f'ρ de Spearman = {num(r.rho, lang, 2)}; n = {int(r.n)}\nsin Región Metropolitana: ρ = {num(rx.rho, lang, 2)}; n = {int(rx.n)}\n{len(z)} comunas visibles; recuentos 1–4 suprimidos', lang),
           transform=d.transAxes, va='top', ha='left', fontsize=6.4, linespacing=1.15)
    d.set_xlabel(text('GRD: eligible episodes per 100 000\nresident person-years, 2021–24', 'GRD: episodios elegibles por 100 000\npersonas-año residentes, 2021–24', lang))
    d.set_ylabel(text('A05: strict-autism entries per 100 000\nresident person-years, 2021–24', 'A05: ingresos autismo estricto por 100 000\npersonas-año residentes, 2021–24', lang))
    d.set_xlim(left=0); d.set_ylim(0, float(z.A05.max()) * 1.25)
    d.legend(loc='upper right', bbox_to_anchor=(1.0, 0.84), fontsize=6.4, handlelength=1.2, borderaxespad=0.2)
    for ax, ch in zip([a, b, c, d], 'abcd'): letter(fig, ax, ch, dx=(-0.19 if ch == 'c' else -0.09))
    save(fig, 'Figure_4', lang, close=False)
    return fig

def figS1(lang):

    # ---- every number of the schematic, recomputed from the tracked tables -------------------
    g = pd.read_csv(TIDY/'grd_year_summary.csv').query("panel=='observed' and activity=='all'")
    gany = g.query("variant=='sin_rett' and position=='any'")
    tot = int(gany.n_episodes_total_same_panel_activity.sum())
    anys = int(gany.n_episodes_f84.sum())
    rett_only = int(g.query("variant=='con_rett' and position=='any'").n_episodes_f84.sum()) - anys
    prin = int(g.query("variant=='sin_rett' and position=='principal'").n_episodes_f84.sum())
    sec = int(g.query("variant=='sin_rett' and position=='secondary_only'").n_episodes_f84.sum())
    st = pd.read_csv(CORPUS/'ST10_grd_f84_subcodes.csv')
    yr0, yr1 = int(gany.year.min()), int(gany.year.max())
    rett_any = int(st[st['ICD-10 subcode'].str.startswith('F84.2') & (st['F84 code position'] == 'Any position')]
                   [[str(y) for y in range(yr0, yr1 + 1)]].iloc[0].astype(str).str.replace(',', '').astype(int).sum())
    rett_kept = rett_any - rett_only
    hosp = gany.set_index('year').hospitals_n
    fixed = int(pd.read_csv(TIDY/'grd_year_summary.csv')
                .query("panel=='fixed65' and activity=='all' and position=='any' and variant=='sin_rett'").hospitals_n.max())

    rp = pd.read_csv(TIDY/'rem_pathway_annual.csv', low_memory=False); rp['code'] = rp.code.astype(str)
    a05 = rp.query("module=='A05' and code=='05990022' and variant=='single_code'").set_index('year').sort_index()
    p2 = rp.query("module=='P2' and code=='P2500500' and measure=='december_stock'").set_index('year').sort_index()
    a_y0, a_y1 = int(a05.era_start.iloc[0]), int(a05.era_end.iloc[0])
    p_y0, p_y1 = int(p2.era_start.iloc[0]), int(p2.era_end.iloc[0])
    a_stable = int(a05.n_stable_panel_establishments.max()); p_stable = int(p2.n_stable_panel_establishments.max())
    a_rep0, a_rep1 = int(a05.n_reporting_establishments.iloc[0]), int(a05.n_reporting_establishments.iloc[-1])
    a_t0, a_t1 = int(a05.total.iloc[0]), int(a05.total.iloc[-1])
    # The plate quotes the P2 stock from the 2021 age-definition break, not from era_start (2019).
    # Like the age lines of box 2, that break year lives only in contenido_v10.json, not in a tracked CSV.
    p_yA = 2021
    p_tA, p_t1 = int(p2.total.loc[p_yA]), int(p2.total.iloc[-1])

    ed = pd.read_csv(TIDY/'education_summary_year.csv').set_index('year')
    pie = ed[ed.pie_harmonised_n.notna()]
    e_y0, e_y1 = int(pie.index.min()), int(pie.index.max())
    split = ed[ed.pie_tea_strict_n.notna() & ed.pie_tea_asperger_n.notna()].index
    s_y0, s_y1 = int(split.min()), int(split.max())
    sinaces = int(ed.index[ed.pie_harmonised_source.fillna('').str.contains('SINACES')].min())
    e_n0, e_n1 = int(pie.pie_harmonised_n.iloc[0]), int(pie.pie_harmonised_n.iloc[-1])

    sv = pd.read_csv(TIDY/'survey_estimates.csv'); tot_rows = sv[sv.subgroup_type == 'total']
    endide = tot_rows[tot_rows.survey.str.startswith('ENDIDE')]
    n_ad = int(endide[(endide.module == 'Adultos (18+)') & (endide.estimate_type == 'primary')].n.iloc[0])
    n_nna = int(endide[endide.module.str.startswith('NNA (2-17)') &
                       (endide.domain == 'ENDIDE NNA 2-17: autismo reportado')].n.iloc[0])
    encavi = tot_rows[tot_rows.survey.str.startswith('ENCAVI')]
    n_val = int(encavi[encavi.estimate_type == 'primary'].n.iloc[0])
    n_base = int(encavi[encavi.estimate_type == 'sensitivity'].n.iloc[0])
    n_exc = n_base - n_val
    endide_lbl = endide.survey.iloc[0].replace('-', '–'); encavi_lbl = encavi.survey.iloc[0].replace('-', '–')

    # ---- panel (a): the three administrative sources, processed in parallel -------------------
    bands = [('grd', 38, 670), ('a05', 716, 1350), ('p2', 1396, 2030)]
    heads = [text('GRD · hospital activity', 'GRD · actividad hospitalaria', lang),
             text('A05 · annual entries', 'A05 · ingresos anuales', lang),

             text('Establishment-month records', 'Registros establecimiento-mes', lang)],
            [f"{p_y0}–{p_y1} · {text('code', 'código', lang)} P2500500",
             text('Autism among NANEAS', 'Autismo en NANEAS', lang)]]
    box2 = [[text('Eligible F84 codes¹', 'Códigos F84 elegibles¹', lang),
             f"{num(anys, lang)} {text('episodes retained', 'episodios incluidos', lang)}",
             f"{num(rett_only, lang)} {text('with Rett and no eligible code', 'con Rett sin código elegible', lang)}",
             text(f'excluded; {num(rett_kept, lang)} with Rett and another',
                  f'excluidos; {num(rett_kept, lang)} con Rett y otro', lang),
             text('eligible code retained', 'código elegible incluidos', lang)],
            [text('Strict autism', 'Autismo estricto', lang),
             text('Sum known monthly totals', 'Sumar totales mensuales conocidos', lang),
             f"{num(a_t0, lang)} ({a_y0}) {text('to', 'a', lang)} {num(a_t1, lang)} ({a_y1})",
             text('Missing cells remain missing', 'Celdas vacías siguen faltantes', lang)],
            # The P2 age universe is stored only as text (contenido_v10.json, manuscript Table 2 and
            # supplement Table S1); no tracked CSV carries it as a value, so it is written out here.
            [text('Select December cut', 'Seleccionar corte de diciembre', lang),
             text('2019–2020: ages 0–9 years', '2019–2020: 0–9 años', lang),
             text('2021–2025: ages 0–19 years', '2021–2025: 0–19 años', lang),
             text('Age-definition break in 2021', 'Quiebre de edad en 2021', lang)]]
    box3 = [[f"Principal: {num(prin, lang)}",
             f"{text('Exclusively secondary', 'Solo secundario', lang)}: {num(sec, lang)}",
             text('Mutually exclusive categories', 'Categorías excluyentes', lang)],
            [f"{num(a_stable, lang)} {text('stable establishments', 'establecimientos estables', lang)}",
             text('≥1 code row each year', '≥1 fila del código cada año', lang),
             f"{num(a_rep0, lang)} → {num(a_rep1, lang)} {text('annual reporters', 'reportantes anuales', lang)}"],
            [f"{num(p_stable, lang)} {text('stable establishments', 'establecimientos estables', lang)}",
             text('December code row every year', 'Fila del código cada diciembre', lang),
             text(f'{p_y0}–{p_y1} membership', f'Pertenencia durante {p_y0}–{p_y1}', lang)]]
    box4 = [[text(f'{num(fixed, lang)} fixed / {num(hosp.min(), lang)}–{num(hosp.max(), lang)} observed hospitals',
                  f'{num(fixed, lang)} hospitales fijos / {num(hosp.min(), lang)}–{num(hosp.max(), lang)} observados', lang),
             text('Coding-depth strata', 'Estratos de profundidad de códigos', lang),
             text('Inpatient / day-case surgery', 'Hospitalización / cirugía ambulatoria', lang),
             text('Matching activity denominator', 'Denominador de actividad propio', lang)],
            [text('Annual flow', 'Flujo anual', lang),
             text('Observed and stable panels', 'Paneles observado y estable', lang),
             text('Age and sex summaries', 'Resúmenes por edad y sexo', lang),
             text('Annual row ≠ full monthly reporting', 'Fila anual ≠ reporte mensual completo', lang)],
            [text('December stock, not a flow', 'Stock de diciembre, no flujo', lang),
             f"{num(p_tA, lang)} ({p_yA}) {text('to', 'a', lang)} {num(p_t1, lang)} ({p_y1})",
             text('Observed / stable / under-10', 'Observado / estable / menores de 10', lang),
             text('June and December never summed', 'Junio y diciembre no se suman', lang)]]
    rows = [(197, 396), (435, 721), (766, 1005), (1032, 1283)]
    for i, (key, bx0, bx1) in enumerate(bands):
        ec, fcb = S1_COLOURS[key]; cx = (bx0 + bx1)/2
        _s1_box(fig, axa, bx0, 118, bx1, 1311, 'none', fc=fcb, lw=0, r=0.05)
        _s1_lines(fig, axa, cx, 153, [heads[i]], size=7.8, color=ec, weight='bold')
        yc = _s1_cyl(fig, axa, bx0 + 26, rows[0][0], bx1 - 26, rows[0][1], ec)
        _s1_lines(fig, axa, cx, yc, cyls[i])
        for (y0, y1), lines in zip(rows[1:], (box2[i], box3[i], box4[i])):
            _s1_box(fig, axa, bx0 + 26, y0, bx1 - 26, y1, ec)

        for (ya, yb) in ((rows[0][1] + 2, rows[1][0] - 2), (rows[1][1] + 2, rows[2][0] - 2), (rows[2][1] + 2, rows[3][0] - 2)):
            _s1_arrow(fig, axa, cx, ya, cx, yb, ec)
    _s1_lines(fig, axa, S1_W/2, 1362,
              [text('Parallel processing; no person-level linkage or observed care cascade',

              size=7.4, color=S1_RED, weight='bold')

    # ---- panel (b): education records and the two household surveys --------------------------

def figS2(lang):
    style(); fig = plt.figure(figsize=(175/25.4, 172/25.4))
    gs = fig.add_gridspec(2, 2, left=0.10, right=0.975, top=0.965, bottom=0.08, hspace=0.50, wspace=0.42)

    # (a) coding-depth strata

    for y, off, col, hatch in ((2019, -0.2, SKY, '//'), (2024, 0.2, BLUE, None)):

        a.bar(x + off, z.rate_per_100k_episodes, width=0.38, color=col, hatch=hatch, edgecolor='white' if hatch is None else BLUE, lw=0.4, label=str(y), zorder=2)
        a.errorbar(x + off, z.rate_per_100k_episodes, yerr=[z.rate_per_100k_episodes - z.rate_lo, z.rate_hi - z.rate_per_100k_episodes], fmt='none', ecolor='#333333', elinewidth=0.6, capsize=1.2, zorder=3)

    a.legend(loc='upper left', fontsize=6.6, handlelength=1.2); a.set_ylim(0, 2300)

    ins.set_ylim(3.5, 7); ins.set_xticks([2019, 2021, 2024]); ins.tick_params(labelsize=6); ins.set_ylabel(text('Mean diagnoses', 'Diagnósticos medios', lang), fontsize=6, labelpad=1)
    ins.legend(fontsize=5.8, loc='lower right', handlelength=1, borderpad=0.2); [ins.spines[s_].set_visible(False) for s_ in ('top', 'right')]
    # (b) activity modality

    ga = pd.read_csv(TIDY/'grd_year_summary.csv').query("variant=='sin_rett' and panel=='observed' and position=='any'")
    for act, col, mk, en, es in (('hospitalisation', GREEN, 's', 'Strict hospitalisation', 'Hospitalización estricta'), ('cma', PINK, '^', 'Major ambulatory surgery', 'Cirugía mayor ambulatoria')):
        z = ga[ga.activity == act].set_index('year').reindex(YRS_GRD)
        b.fill_between(z.index, z.rate_lo, z.rate_hi, color=col, alpha=0.15, lw=0); b.plot(z.index, z.rate_per_100k_episodes, color=col, marker=mk, label=text(en, es, lang))

    b.set_ylabel(text('Eligible episodes per 100 000\nepisodes of each modality', 'Episodios elegibles por 100 000\nepisodios de cada modalidad', lang)); b.legend(loc='upper left', fontsize=6.6, handlelength=1.4)

title: 4  GRD: hospital epidemiology and diagnostic trajectories of autism
text:
5 Part A. Epidemiology of hospitalisations with an ASD code
This report has two parts. Part A describes the epidemiology of hospitalisations carrying an autism spectrum disorder (ASD) code in GRD (Grupos Relacionados por el Diagnóstico), the public-hospital discharge database grouped by diagnosis-related groups: how many there are, how they evolve, who has them, where they live, what the episodes look like and which other diagnoses accompany them. Part B reconstructs the coding trajectories: which hospital diagnoses appear before the first observed autism record, and in which position it is recorded. Definitions, denominators and methods are in Methods; here only the caveats needed to read each result are repeated.
The main definition is operational ASD (F84.0, F84.1, F84.5, F84.8 and F84.9 in any of the 35 diagnostic positions). Rates are expressed per 100 000 person-years of the INE (national statistics institute) population and are age-standardised to the WHO world standard population. No rate in this report is an incidence or prevalence of autism: they are rates of hospitalisations, or of hospitalised persons, carrying the code in public facilities with the GRD system.

def feature_table(variable, caption, top=None, labels=None, years=(2019, 2022, last_year)):
    frame = main_features.loc[main_features.variable == variable].groupby(["year", "value"]).records.sum().unstack("year").fillna(0)
    frame["Total 2019–2024"] = frame.sum(axis=1)
    frame = frame.sort_values("Total 2019–2024", ascending=False)
    if top:
        frame = frame.head(top)
    for year in years:
        frame[f"% {year}"] = 100 * frame[year] / frame[year].sum()
    frame["% 2019–2024"] = 100 * frame["Total 2019–2024"] / frame["Total 2019–2024"].sum()
    frame = frame.reset_index().rename(columns={"value": "Category"})
    labels = {**VALUE_LABELS, **(labels or {})}
    frame["Category"] = frame.Category.map(lambda v: labels.get(v, v))
    columns = ["Category"] + [y for y in years] + ["Total 2019–2024"] + [f"% {y}" for y in years] + ["% 2019–2024"]

los_summary = read_result("grd_epi_los_summary.csv")
los_age = read_result("grd_epi_los_age.csv")

def pooled_los(frame, keys):
    """Exact quantiles are not additive across roles; means and totals are pooled, quantiles come from the widest stratum."""
    rows = []
    for values, group in frame.groupby(keys):
        values = values if isinstance(values, tuple) else (values,)
        n = group.n.sum()
        widest = group.loc[group.n.idxmax()]
        rows.append(dict(zip(keys, values)) | dict(n=n, media=(group["mean"] * group.n).sum() / n if n else np.nan,
                                                  mediana=widest["median"], q25=widest.q25, q75=widest.q75, p90=widest.p90,
                                                  dias_totales=group.total_days.sum(), pct_estancia_0=100 * group.n_los0.sum() / n if n else np.nan))
    return pd.DataFrame(rows)

The regions with the highest rates (Ñuble, Magallanes, Arica y Parinacota, Biobío, Antofagasta) combine hospitals with a large regional catchment and probably more exhaustive coding practices; the Metropolitan Region shows low rates despite having the largest absolute number of records.     ax.axhline(0, color="#999999", linewidth=.8); ax.axvline(0, color="#999999", linewidth=.8)

Significant positive autocorrelation indicates that communes with high ratios tend to neighbour other communes with high ratios. High-high clusters are concentrated in Ñuble and Biobío, around Chillán and Greater Concepción; low-low clusters in the Metropolitan Region, Valparaíso, O’Higgins and Coquimbo. The FDR-corrected reading reduces the clusters to the most robust ones: the Ñuble-Biobío core and a few low-ratio communes in the Metropolitan Region. These patterns describe the geography of hospital recording and are consistent with the organisation of the care network and with the catchment of the Chillán and Concepción hospitals.

title: 4  GRD: hospital epidemiology and diagnostic trajectories of autism
text:
6.1 B1. Question and definition
Which hospital diagnoses appear before the first observed autism record, and when is it recorded as principal or secondary?
The primary analysis uses the operational definition F84.0, F84.1, F84.5, F84.8 and F84.9 in any of the 35 diagnostic positions. All discharges of those identifiers are retrieved, including those without F84. Comparisons are also made with specific F84.0 and with historical F84.
The index date is the first observed discharge with the selected definition. Age refers to admission in that episode. The date of clinical diagnosis is unknown, and autism may have been diagnosed earlier, in outpatient care or outside the available period.
DIAGNOSTICO1 is used operationally as the principal diagnosis and DIAGNOSTICO2–35 as secondary diagnoses. A prior diagnosis may be a comorbidity, a symptom, an independent reason for admission or an alternative diagnosis. The sequence of codes does not demonstrate that these were clinical differentials that were ruled out.

])

7.1 Reproducibility and next extension
This QMD runs the descriptive statistics and figures in Python from the aggregated outputs of scripts/grd_epidemiology.py, scripts/epi_rates.py and scripts/grd_trajectories.py. The linkage audit comes from scripts/audit_grd_linkage.py. The dictionary of the derived tables is in output_files/consolidacion/README.md and the execution instructions are in the repository README.
The pending extensions are: confirming the linkage and the position semantics with the data producer, restricting the cohort by opportunity for observation, comparing principal/secondary position with adjustment for age, sex, year, contacts and hospital, incorporating deaths (DEIS) and emergency care, and validating a sample of clinical records to distinguish comorbidity, recording error and differential diagnosis.

title: 5  REM: autism in outpatient care, screening and rehabilitation
text:
5.1 What REM measures
REM (Resúmenes Estadísticos Mensuales), the monthly statistical summaries of the public network, contains aggregated records of care activity: each row is a facility, a month and a service code. A mental-health programme entry does not necessarily represent a new diagnosis, a programme discharge does not describe the outcome of a cohort of entries, and no figure corresponds to unique persons nationally. These counts do not estimate incidence, prevalence, retention or individual times to diagnosis. The population rates presented below are rates of recorded entries, an indicator of access and activity in the public system.
The extraction reads the canonical Series A files and applies each year’s dictionaries. The generic pervasive developmental disorder (PDD) codes of 2017–2020 are kept separate from the specific codes available from 2021. The Methods page details the reading rules; the table below summarises them.
total_known adds up only the rows that have a complete total according to that rule. It may be a partial sum when fields are missing; it does not automatically replace the national total. Sums of observed cells are identified as such.

Programme entries are lower in January, February and December, months of holidays and reduced outpatient activity, and higher between March and November. The pattern reflects how facilities operate, not the occurrence of autism.


5.2.3 Entry rates by population
The rates use the reported age and sex cells (Col04 to Col37) as numerator and the INE (national statistics institute) population of the year as denominator; they are age-standardised to the WHO world standard population and accompanied by 95% gamma intervals. They are rates of recorded entries, not of persons or of new cases.

text:
5.4 Facility panel
A facility appears in the series only in the months with a row for the code; in practice, A05 rows almost always carry a positive value, so “months with a row” is equivalent to months with reported activity. The stable panel gathers the facilities with at least one autism entry reported in each of the years 2021–2024; it allows checking whether the trend is explained by the incorporation of new reporters.


Show the code that produced this
pan = panel.loc[panel.code == AUTISM].copy()
years_present = pan.groupby("IdEstablecimiento").year.nunique()
stable_ids = set(years_present.index[years_present == 4])
pan["panel"] = np.where(pan.IdEstablecimiento.isin(stable_ids), "Stable panel", "Other")
summary = pan.groupby(["year", "panel"]).agg(facilities=("IdEstablecimiento", "nunique"), entries=("Col01", "sum")).unstack("panel").fillna(0)
summary.columns = [f"{a} · {b}" for a, b in summary.columns]
summary["Total facilities"] = pan.groupby("year").IdEstablecimiento.nunique()
summary["Total entries"] = pan.groupby("year").Col01.sum()
summary["% of entries in stable panel"] = 100 * summary["entries · Stable panel"] / summary["Total entries"]

section: 5.5 A03: screening and suspicion in well-child check-ups
text:
5.5 A03: screening and suspicion in well-child check-ups
There is a change of instrument and of age headings: the reviewed sections distinguish the MCHAT series 2019–2022 and M-CHAT R/F 2023–2024; in 2024 a section for 31 to 59 months also appears. Check-ups, administration of the instrument, results of each stage and referral must be distinguished. The ratios presented only relate codes from the same section, instrument and stage; none is a population positivity rate, because the denominators are not all screened children. The sums use the observed male and female cells; the complete-rows column indicates how many rows reported both sexes.

5.5.1 MCHAT series, 2019–2022


Show the code that produced this
a03 = annual.loc[annual.sheet == "A03"].copy()
a03["observed"] = a03[["Col01", "Col02"]].sum(axis=1, min_count=1)
labels_old = {"03500404": "18-month check-ups", "03500405": "With language and/or social impairment", "03500406": "MCHAT screening performed (with impairment)", "03500407": "Abnormal MCHAT screening (with impairment)"}
old = a03.loc[a03.code.isin(labels_old) & (a03.year <= 2022)].pivot(index="year", columns="code", values="observed")
old_sex = a03.loc[a03.code.isin(labels_old) & (a03.year <= 2022)].pivot(index="year", columns="code", values=["Col01", "Col02"])
table = pd.DataFrame({"Year": old.index})
for code, label in labels_old.items():
    table[label] = old[code].values
table["% with impairment among check-ups"] = 100 * old["03500405"].values / old["03500404"].values
table["% screened among those with impairment"] = 100 * old["03500406"].values / old["03500405"].values
table["% abnormal among screened"] = 100 * old["03500407"].values / old["03500406"].values
table["% abnormal among check-ups"] = 100 * old["03500407"].values / old["03500404"].values
show_table(table, "Section F, MCHAT 2019–2022: sums of observed cells (males + females) and ratios between stages", {c: 1 for c in table.columns if c.startswith("%")})
sex_old = pd.DataFrame({"Year": old.index})
for code, label in labels_old.items():
    sex_old[f"{label} · M"] = old_sex[("Col01", code)].values
    sex_old[f"{label} · F"] = old_sex[("Col02", code)].values
sex_old["M:F ratio check-ups"] = old_sex[("Col01", "03500404")].values / old_sex[("Col02", "03500404")].values
sex_old["M:F ratio abnormal"] = old_sex[("Col01", "03500407")].values / old_sex[("Col02", "03500407")].values
show_table(sex_old, "MCHAT series by sex and male:female ratio of check-ups and of abnormal screenings", {"M:F ratio check-ups": 2, "M:F ratio abnormal": 2})

section: 5.7 Ecological comparison between REM and GRD
text:
5.7 Ecological comparison between REM and GRD
REM entry rates (facility region or commune) and GRD hospitalisation rates (residence) are compared by region and year and, further below, by commune. They measure different activities with different units; the correlation describes only the territorial coherence between sources.

5.7.1 Regional correlation


Show the code that produced this
years = sorted(ecological.year.dropna().unique())
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, len(years), figsize=(12, 3.6), layout="constrained", sharey=False)
corr_rows = []
for ax, year in zip(np.atleast_1d(axes), years):
    frame = ecological.loc[ecological.year == year]
    rho, p = stats.spearmanr(frame.rem_asr, frame.grd_persons_asr)
    corr_rows.append(dict(Year=int(year), Regions=len(frame), **{"Spearman ρ": rho, "p value": p}))
    ax.scatter(frame.rem_asr, frame.grd_persons_asr, color=COLORS[0])
    for _, row in frame.iterrows():
        ax.annotate(REGION_NAMES.get(int(row.cut_region), "")[:8], (row.rem_asr, row.grd_persons_asr), fontsize=6, xytext=(2, 2), textcoords="offset points")
    ax.set(title=f"{int(year)} · ρ = {rho:.2f}", xlabel="REM: entries per 100 000 (ASR)", ylabel="GRD: persons per 100 000 (ASR)")
plt.show()
show_table(pd.DataFrame(corr_rows), "Spearman correlation between regional REM and GRD rates by year", {"Spearman ρ": 2, "p value": 3})

The correlations are positive and weak: the regions with the most outpatient entries are not necessarily those with the most hospitalisations, because outpatient supply, hospital supply and recording practices vary independently. Atacama, with very high entry rates and low hospitalisations, illustrates that dissociation.


5.7.2 Commune-level correlation
At the commune scale the comparison is more demanding: REM assigns entries to the facility commune and GRD to the commune of residence, so a commune without a facility reporting the code has no REM entries even if its residents are hospitalised. As REM only provides totals by commune, both sources are compared with crude rates per 100 000 person-years and with indirect standardised ratios, that is, observed over expected according to the national sex- and age-specific rates of the same source and period: the standardised entry ratio (SER) in REM and the standardised hospitalisation ratio (SHR) in GRD. The main analysis uses the continental communes with at least one reporting facility; as sensitivity analyses, it adds the communes with at least 20 entries and 20 hospitalised persons, where rates are more stable, and all continental communes with zero imputed to those that did not report.


Show the code that produced this
pool = ecological_com.loc[(ecological_com.period == "2021-2024") & ecological_com.continental].copy()
informantes = pool.loc[pool.rem_reported]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 5), layout="constrained")
sizes = 6 + 60 * informantes.population / informantes.population.max()
labelled = informantes.sort_values("rem_ingresos", ascending=False).head(6)
panels = [(axes[0], "rem_crude", "grd_persons_crude", "REM: entries per 100 000 person-years", "GRD: hospitalised persons per 100 000", "Crude rates", None),
          (axes[1], "rem_sir", "grd_persons_sir", "REM: standardised entry ratio (SER)", "GRD: standardised hospitalisation ratio (SHR)", "Indirect standardised ratios", 1.0)]
for ax, x, y, xlabel, ylabel, title, reference in panels:
    rho, p = stats.spearmanr(informantes[x], informantes[y], nan_policy="omit")
    positive = informantes.loc[(informantes[x] > 0) & (informantes[y] > 0)]
    ax.scatter(positive[x], positive[y], s=sizes.loc[positive.index], color=COLORS[0], alpha=.55, edgecolor="white", linewidth=.3)
    for _, row in labelled.iterrows():
        if row[x] > 0 and row[y] > 0:
            ax.annotate(row.comuna, (row[x], row[y]), fontsize=7, xytext=(3, 3), textcoords="offset points")
    if reference is not None:
        ax.axhline(reference, color="#999999", linestyle="--", linewidth=1)
        ax.axvline(reference, color="#999999", linestyle="--", linewidth=1)
    ax.set(title=f"{title} · ρ = {rho:.2f} (n = {len(informantes)})", xlabel=xlabel, ylabel=ylabel, xscale="log", yscale="log")
plt.show()

Communes with zero in either source do not appear on the logarithmic scale but are included in the correlation.







Show the code that produced this
def spearman_row(frame, period, subset):
    row = {"Period": period, "Communes": subset, "n": len(frame)}
    for label, x, y in [("entries–persons", "rem_crude", "grd_persons_crude"), ("SER–SHR", "rem_sir", "grd_persons_sir"),
                        ("entries–records", "rem_crude", "grd_records_crude")]:
        rho, p = stats.spearmanr(frame[x], frame[y], nan_policy="omit")
        row[f"ρ {label}"] = rho
        row[f"p {label}"] = p
    return row
rows = []
for period in list(dict.fromkeys(ecological_com.period)):
    frame = ecological_com.loc[(ecological_com.period == period) & ecological_com.continental]
    reported = frame.loc[frame.rem_reported]
    rows.append(spearman_row(reported, period, "With a reporting facility"))
    rows.append(spearman_row(reported.loc[(reported.rem_ingresos >= 20) & (reported.grd_persons >= 20)], period, "≥ 20 entries and ≥ 20 persons"))
    rows.append(spearman_row(frame.assign(rem_crude=frame.rem_crude.fillna(0.0), rem_sir=frame.rem_sir.fillna(0.0)), period, "All (no row = 0)"))
corr_com = pd.DataFrame(rows)
decimals = {c: 2 for c in corr_com.columns if c.startswith("ρ")} | {c: 3 for c in corr_com.columns if c.startswith("p ")}
show_table(corr_com, "Spearman correlation between commune-level REM and GRD rates by period and set of continental communes", decimals)

Continental communes with at least one facility reporting autism entries in 2021–2024: 321 of 342; with at least 20 entries and 20 hospitalised persons: 119. The SER uses the national sex- and age-specific entry rates of REM as reference; the SHR, the national rates of hospitalised persons of GRD.


The commune-level correlation is positive and weak among the communes with a reporting facility (ρ close to 0.3 in 2021–2024 and between 0.1 and 0.25 in individual years), similar with crude rates and with standardised ratios, and rises to about 0.6 when the analysis is restricted to communes with at least 20 entries and 20 hospitalised persons, where rates depend less on chance. Including all communes with zero imputed raises the correlation for a different reason: the communes without a reporting facility are mostly small and also have few hospitalisations. Chillán combines the highest rates of both sources, while Copiapó reproduces the Atacama dissociation, with very high outpatient entries and low hospitalisations. The difference in territorial unit, facility versus residence, shifts entries towards the communes that concentrate outpatient supply and by itself limits the coherence that can be expected.

6.1 Reproducibility
This QMD performs the groupings, tables and figures in Python. The prior extraction and dictionary validation correspond to scripts/audit_rem.py; the population rates to scripts/epi_rates.py; the outputs are documented in output_files/consolidacion/README.md. 6.10 The earliest analysis
This chapter holds every result table the study produced, read from docs/study/data/. They ship with the repository, so each one can be opened, checked and reused without the source microdata. Each table below unfolds to show its full contents.
The study was written over several rounds of revision. Each round added tables without ever changing one that had already been computed, so what appears here is the union of all of them — a single result set, not a sequence of drafts. That claim is checked rather than asserted: scripts/audit_versions.py hashes every table of every round and compares them pairwise.

different observation window and a different definition, and a reader should not place them side by side

record of what was found, not because they extend the series.

title: 6  Result tables
